### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.1, printed page 151 (PDF pages
160–161), item `awodey:7.1:construction-cat-equalizer` — the equalizer of two
parallel functors `F, G : C ⟶ D` in `Cat`, built explicitly as the subcategory
of `C` spanned by the objects and arrows on which `F` and `G` agree, with the
evident inclusion as the equalizing functor (Awodey leaves the verification to
the reader). Same obligation as the equalizer half of small-completeness of
`Cat`; Awodey uses it as his running example of a subcategory.

What this section adds beyond the abstract limit:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.1) Present the equalizer concretely as a
      `Construction/Subcategory.v` subcategory of `C` (agreeing objects and
      agreeing arrows), and prove the inclusion is the equalizing functor —
      not merely that some limit exists.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.1, printed page 151 (PDF pages
160–161), item `awodey:7.1:remark-cat-complete` — the prose recollection that
`Cat` has an initial category 0, binary coproducts, a terminal category 1,
binary products, all small products and coproducts, and (with the explicit
equalizer construction) all limits.

In-tree today only the finite half exists: `Instance/Cat/Cartesian.v:39`
(`Cat_Cartesian`), `Instance/Cat/Cocartesian.v:40` (`Cat_Cocartesian`),
`Instance/One.v:54` (`Cat_Terminal`), `Instance/Zero.v:44` (`Cat_Initial`);
`Structure/Complete.v:115` defines `Complete {C} := ∀ D (F : D ⟶ C), Limit F`
and is never instantiated at `Cat`. The small-coproducts clause is already
filed as #338.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.1) Small/indexed products of a family of categories
      (only the binary and nullary cases exist in-tree).
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.1) A `Complete Cat` witness assembling small products
      with the equalizer construction.
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.1) Record the book's caveat that coequalizers of
      categories are much harder to describe (already for posets), so that the
      colimit side is explicitly scoped rather than silently omitted.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.1, printed page 153 (PDF page 162),
item `awodey:7.1:construction-linear-representation` — a functor `R : G ⟶ C`
out of a group regarded as a one-object category is a general notion of
representation of `G` in `C`; when `C` is finite-dimensional real vector
spaces and linear maps this is exactly a linear representation, assigning an
invertible matrix to each group element and matrix multiplication to the group
operation. Same obligation as the functor-category presentation of linear
representations.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.1) The degenerate case: a functor from a group into a
      poset is trivial (all arrows are forced to be identities).

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.1, printed page 154 (PDF page 163),
item `awodey:7.1:construction-poset-to-group` — a functor `g : P ⟶ G` from a
poset to a group (both as categories) is exactly an assignment of a group
element `g_{p,q}` to each pair `p ≤ q` satisfying `g_{p,p} = u` and
`g_{q,r} · g_{p,q} = g_{p,r}`, the object part being forced because `G` has one
object. Same obligation as classifying functors between preorders and groups.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.1) The cocycle characterization itself: functors
      `Poset P ⟶ Deloop G` correspond exactly to families `g_{p,q}` satisfying
      the unit and composition conditions, proved in both directions.
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.1) The worked witness `P = (ℝ, ≤)`, `G = (ℝ, +)`,
      `g_{x,y} = y − x`, verifying the two conditions.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.2, printed page 154 (PDF page 163),
item `awodey:7.2:def-generator` — an object `C` of a locally small category is
a generator (separator) when the representable `Hom_C(C,−)` is faithful,
equivalently when parallel arrows are distinguished by their effect on
generalized elements based at `C`. Same obligation as generating/separating
sets of objects.

In-tree today the only counterpart is the *dual*, and only in family form and
only as an input datum to SAFT: `Adjunction/SAFT.v:99`
`Record Cogenerator { cog_index; cog_obj; cog_separates ... }`, whose header
(`:94-98`) describes it as "the representables `C(−, cog_obj j)` are jointly
faithful" without proving that reading.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The covariant single-object notion `Generator`
      (separation by arrows *out of* a fixed object), not only the cogenerating
      family.
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The equivalence `C is a generator ⟺ Faithful [Hom C,−]`
      linking the elementwise condition to `Theory/Functor.v:342` and
      `Functor/Hom.v:60` — currently only paraphrased in a header comment.
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The witnesses: the terminal object generates `Sets`,
      and the free group on one generator generates `Grp`.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.2, printed page 154 (PDF pages
163–164), item `awodey:7.2:construction-free-group-natural-iso` — the functor
represented by the free group on one generator is isomorphic to the forgetful
functor: `Hom_Grp(F(1), G) ≅ U(G)` for each group `G`, compatibly with every
homomorphism `h : G → H` (post-composition `h_*` versus `U(h)`). This is the
book's first named instance of an isomorphism "natural in `G`". Same obligation
as the free-group functor and its adjunction.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) Exhibit `U : Grp ⟶ Sets` as *representable*, i.e.
      construct the natural isomorphism `Hom_Grp(F(1), −) ≅ U` (the library's
      `Functor/Representable.v:46` `Representable` class is currently never
      instantiated for any `Sets`-valued functor).

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.2, printed page 155 (PDF page 164),
item `awodey:7.2:remark-representables-preserve-limits` — the passing remark
that representable functors necessarily preserve all limits, so `U : Grp ⟶ Sets`
does too, and that faithfulness of that representable is the precise form of
the informal claim that `Grp` is concrete. Same obligation as the continuity of
hom-functors.

The `Grp`-specific consequence is already covered by #411 (the forgetful
functor of `Grp` lifts and creates limits, hence preserves them), and the
concreteness vocabulary by #263 and #644.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) Transport along a natural isomorphism: a functor
      naturally isomorphic to a representable preserves limits — the step the
      remark actually uses to get from `Hom(F(1),−)` to `U`.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.2, Example 7.3, printed page 155 (PDF
pages 164–165), item `awodey:7.2:example3` — if `G` is a group object in a
locally small category `C`, the contravariant representable `Hom_C(−, G)`
carries a group structure on each hom-set, lifting to a functor `C^op ⟶ Grp`;
in `Sets` the structure is pointwise, and precomposition `h*` is checked to be
a homomorphism. Same obligation as characterizing group objects through their
representable functors.

In-tree today the nearest artifact is `Structure/Monoid.v:290`
`Hom_Monoid {x} `(Y : Monoid y) : @MonoidObject C CC_Monoidal (y ^ x)` — a
*monoid* structure on the *internal* exponential, requiring cartesian closure.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The group case: an analogue of `Hom_Monoid` for
      `Structure/Group.v:109`'s `GroupObject` (`rg 'Hom_Group|GroupHom'`
      currently returns 0 hits).
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The *external* hom-set formulation — a group structure
      on the setoid `Hom_C(X, G)` with no cartesian-closure hypothesis — and the
      functorial lift `C^op ⟶ Grp`, with precomposition proved a homomorphism.
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The concrete computation `Hom_Sets(X, G) ≅ ∏_{x∈X} G`.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.2, printed page 156 (PDF page 165),
item `awodey:7.2:remark-equational-structure-transfers` — the general moral of
the preceding example: structure defined by operations and equations is
retained when passing to hom-objects, while properties given by non-equational
conditions need not be (the counterexample being that ℝ is a field but the ring
of continuous real functions on ℝ is not, since the pointwise inverse of
`x ↦ x²` is discontinuous at 0). Same obligation family as transferring
algebraic structure through representables.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The general positive half, stated once rather than
      per-theory: a model of a Lawvere theory composed with a finite-product-
      preserving functor is again a model (`Theory/Lawvere/Model.v:50`
      `Record Model` is the natural home; no such closure lemma exists).
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) The negative half, or an explicit scoping note: a
      witness that a non-equational condition fails to transfer. The book's own
      witness needs the reals, topology and fields, none of which exist in-tree
      (see #275 for the `C(X)` functor); if no in-tree witness is built, the
      file header must say so.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.2, printed page 156 (PDF page 165),
item `awodey:7.2:construction-continuous-real-functions-ring` — for a space `X`,
`C(X) = Hom_Top(X, ℝ)` is a ring under the pointwise operations inherited from
ℝ, and precomposition along a continuous `h : Y → X` is a ring homomorphism,
giving `C : Top^op ⟶ Rings`. Same obligation as the ring of continuous
functions as a contravariant functor.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.2) Derive the functoriality *from representability* —
      recognize `C(X)` as the hom-set `Hom_Top(X, ℝ)` with the ring structure
      transferred from the ring object ℝ, rather than checking the functor laws
      by hand; this is the route the section uses and it connects the item to
      the representable-lifting story (#341).

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.3, printed page 158 (PDF page 167),
item `awodey:7.3:def-ultrafilter` — an ultrafilter in a Boolean algebra `B` is
a proper subset `U ⊆ B` containing 1, closed under meets, upward closed, and
maximal among proper filters. Same definition as the one already filed here
(§2.3 states it for the same purpose, and §7.3 restates it as the input to the
Stone development).

No new formalizable aspect: the four clauses and the correspondence with
Boolean homomorphisms to 2 are already inside this issue's scope. Chapter 7
only adds downstream consumers, which are filed separately (the ultrafilter
functor and the Stone representation).

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.3, printed page 158 (PDF page 167),
item `awodey:7.3:remark-ultrafilter-maximality` — the observation (posed as an
exercise) that maximality of a filter `U` in a Boolean algebra is equivalent to
primeness: for every `x` either `x ∈ U` or `¬x ∈ U`. Same obligation family as
the filters/ultrafilters definitions already filed here.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.3) The equivalence *maximality ⟺ primeness* proved in
      both directions — the characterization every later Stone argument
      actually uses.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.5, Example 7.7, printed page 163 (PDF
page 172), item `awodey:7.5:example7` — the insertion of generators
`η_X : X → U M(X)`, sending an element to the corresponding one-letter word,
is natural in `X`, because the induced homomorphism `M(f)` is determined by its
action on generators. Same obligation as the free monoid and its universal
property.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.5) Package the insertion of generators as a natural
      transformation `η : Id_Sets ⟹ U ◯ M` (a `Transform`, with the naturality
      square proved), not only as the universal-arrow component. The generic
      fact holds for every adjunction
      (`Adjunction/Natural/Transformation/Universal.v:84`), but the free-monoid
      instance of it is what this example asks for and no monoid free/forgetful
      adjunction exists in-tree.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.5, Example 7.12, printed pages 165–167
(PDF pages 174–176), item `awodey:7.5:example12` — the dual space functor
`(−)* = Vect(−, ℝ) : Vect^op ⟶ Vect`, the canonical map `η_V : V → V**`,
`x ↦ ev_x`, its naturality, and the punchline that `η_V` is an isomorphism
exactly for finite-dimensional `V` while `V ≅ V*` holds pointwise but not
naturally. Same obligation as the double-dual natural isomorphism for
finite-dimensional vector spaces.

The in-tree double-dual apparatus *assumes* what this example constructs:
`Structure/Monoidal/StarAutonomous.v:252` defines
`double_dual (d : C) : C ⟶ C := dual d ◯ (dual d)^op`, and the class at `:261`
posits `star_double_dual {x : C} : x ≅ double_dual dualizer x` as a field
(the file header at `:71-78` says so, and no concrete model is provided).

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.5) Construct the canonical map `η_x : x → x**` as the
      double transpose of evaluation and prove it natural, instead of positing
      an unspecified isomorphism plus its naturality.
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.5) The contrast that makes the example a *motivation* for
      naturality: `V ≅ V*` for finite-dimensional `V` but not naturally, versus
      the natural `V ≅ V**`.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.6, Lemma 7.14 (the bifunctor lemma),
printed page 168 (PDF pages 177–178), item `awodey:7.6:lem14` — object and
arrow maps `F₀ : A₀ × B₀ → C₀`, `F₁ : A₁ × B₁ → C₁` constitute a functor
`A ∏ B ⟶ C` if and only if `F` is functorial in each argument separately and
satisfies the interchange law
`F(A',β) ∘ F(α,B) = F(α,B') ∘ F(A,β)`. Same obligation as building bifunctors
and transformations from partial data.

In-tree only the necessity direction exists, as the `bimap` calculus of
`Functor/Bifunctor.v` (`bimap_id_id:59`, `bimap_comp:68`,
`bimap_comp_id_left:80`, `bimap_comp_id_right:91`, `bimap_id_right_left:104`,
`bimap_id_left_right:116`). Sufficiency is reachable only by first building a
functor into a functor category and applying `Cat_Closed`'s `exp_iso`
(`Instance/Cat/Cartesian/Closed.v:47`), which also pins all three categories to
one universe level of `Cat`.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.6) A smart constructor over RAW data —
      `Build_Bifunctor : (object map) → (two separately functorial actions) →
      (interchange law) → C ∏ D ⟶ E` — and the statement of the lemma as an
      *iff* over that raw data, so users need not route through `[B, C]`.
      (`Construction/Funny.v:377`'s `Record SepFunctorial` is the closest raw-
      data record but by design imposes no interchange condition and eliminates
      into `C □ D`.)

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.7, Example 7.15, printed page 171 (PDF
page 180), item `awodey:7.7:example15` — the elementary functor categories:
`C^1 = C`; `C^2` for the walking arrow 2 is the arrow category; and for a
discrete index `I`, `C^I` is the `I`-indexed power of `C`. Same obligation as
identifying the arrow category with `[2, B]`; the discrete-index clause is
already filed as #276.

Relevant in-tree state: `Construction/Arrow.v:110` defines
`Arrow {C} : Category := (Id[C] ↓ Id[C])` and its header explicitly discloses
that "no formal comparison with a functor category over the walking arrow
`[_2]` of `Instance/Two.v` is developed in-tree".

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.7) The `C^1 ≅ C` clause stated at the level of `Cat`:
      instantiate `Structure/Cartesian/Closed.v:389`'s generic `exp_one` at
      `Instance/Cat/Cartesian/Closed.v:47`'s `Cat_Closed` and record the
      resulting isomorphism `[1, C] ≅ C`, which is nowhere stated in-tree.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.7, Example 7.16, printed page 171 (PDF
pages 180–181), item `awodey:7.7:example16` — the "transcendental deduction":
using only the exponential adjunction in `Cat`, the objects of `D^C` are forced
to be functors `C ⟶ D` and its arrows to be functors `C × 2 ⟶ D`, i.e. natural
transformations. Same obligation as the cylinder `C × 2` and the universal
natural transformation; the `1 ⟶ X` and `2 ⟶ X` correspondences it chains
through are already filed as #233.

The library *posits* natural transformations as the morphisms of `Fun`
(`Instance/Fun.v:108`) rather than deducing them, and the intermediate
correspondences appear only as header prose (`Instance/Two.v:83`: "a natural
transformation between two functors from C to D is a functor from C ∏ [_2] to
D, a directed homotopy").

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.7) The transposed form of the same correspondence:
      functors `C ⟶ D^2` (into the arrow category) correspond to natural
      transformations, obtained from the cylinder form by `Cat_Closed`'s
      `exp_iso` (`Instance/Cat/Cartesian/Closed.v:47`) — the step that makes
      the deduction of `D^C`'s arrows go through.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.7, Example 7.21, printed page 175 (PDF
page 184), item `awodey:7.7:example21` — for groups `G, H` as one-object
categories, a natural transformation between homomorphisms `f, g : G → H` is a
single element `h ∈ H` with `f(x)·h = h·g(x)`, i.e. conjugation by `h` carrying
`f` to `g`. Same obligation as classifying natural transformations between
group homomorphisms as conjugations.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.7) The consequence Awodey draws: every such
      transformation is invertible (its inverse is conjugation by `h⁻¹`), so
      the functor category `H^G` is a **groupoid** — and in general not a
      group, since it usually has many objects.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.7, printed page 175 (PDF page 184),
item `awodey:7.7:def-groupoid` — a groupoid is a category in which every arrow
is an isomorphism; groups are exactly the one-object groupoids, and groupoids
arise in topology as the paths between different points of a space. Same
definition as the one already filed here.

In-tree the name is bound to a *construction*, not to the property:
`Construction/Groupoid.v:103`
`Program Definition Groupoid (C : Category) : Category := {| obj := @obj C; hom := @Isomorphism C; homset := @iso_setoid C; id := @iso_id C; compose := @iso_compose C |}`
— the core of `C`. `rg -i 'IsGroupoid|is_groupoid'` finds only the header
comment at line 13.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.7) A groupoid **predicate** on an arbitrary category
      ("every morphism is an isomorphism"), so that statements can be
      quantified over groupoids at all — without it, `Grpd` cannot be cut out
      and nothing can be said of a groupoid that is not the core of something.
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.7) The lemma that every arrow of `Groupoid C` is
      invertible (`iso_sym` is available in `Theory/Isomorphism.v` but is never
      applied to state this).
- [ ] (from Awodey §7.7) The identification of groups with one-object
      groupoids.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.8, Example 7.23, printed pages 176–177
(PDF pages 185–186), item `awodey:7.8:example23` — choosing for each finite set
`A` an ordinal `|A|` and an isomorphism `θ_A : A → i|A|` makes `|−|` a functor
`Sets_fin ⟶ Ord_fin` and the `θ_A` the components of a natural isomorphism
`Id ≅ i ◯ |−|`, while in the other order `θ_n = 1_n` gives `|i(−)| = Id`
strictly. Same obligation as the skeleton equivalence between finite sets and
finite ordinals.

In-tree only one side exists: `Instance/FinSet.v:116`
`Program Definition FinSet : Category := {| obj := nat; hom := fun m n => Fin.t m → Fin.t n; ... |}`
is `Ord_fin`; there is no category of finite sets, no finiteness predicate on
setoids, and `Theory/Equivalence.v:98` confines skeletons to concrete instances
such as this one.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.8) The **asymmetry** of the two round trips: the chosen
      isomorphism family `θ` gives only a natural isomorphism `Id ≅ i ◯ |−|`,
      whereas `|i(−)| = Id` holds strictly — the concrete illustration of why
      equivalence, not isomorphism, is the right notion.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.8, unnumbered remark, printed page 178
(PDF page 187), item `awodey:7.8:remark-setsfin-ordfin` — `Sets_fin` is
equivalent to `Ord_fin` because (1) the inclusion `i` is essentially surjective
(every finite set is isomorphic to some `i(n)`) and (2) `i` is full and
faithful; Awodey notes these two conditions characterize equivalences in
general. Same obligation as the skeleton equivalence already filed here; the
general criterion it points forward to is fully in-tree
(`Theory/Equivalence/FullFaithful.v:160` `FF_ESO_Equivalence`,
`Theory/Equivalence.v:141` `EssentiallySurjective`).

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.8) Discharge the two characteristic conditions *for this
      instance*: the inclusion of finite sets into finite ordinals is full and
      faithful (hom-set bijection) and essentially surjective ("every finite
      set is isomorphic to some `Fin.t n`"), and derive the equivalence via
      `FF_ESO_Equivalence` rather than by hand.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.9, Example 7.26, printed page 181 (PDF
page 190), item `awodey:7.9:example26` — the two categories used in the
following proposition: `Par` (sets and partial functions, composition via the
pullback of the domain-of-definition inclusion) and `Sets_*` (pointed sets and
point-preserving maps). The `Sets_*` half is the same obligation as the
category of pointed sets already filed here; the `Par` half, including its
pullback presentation, is filed as #678.

In-tree `Par` exists twice (`Instance/Sets/Par.v:27` `Part` over setoids,
`Instance/Coq/Par.v:53` `Par` over `Type`), both via the Kleisli-of-`option`
encoding. `Sets_*` is never constructed, although `Construction/Slice.v:169`
defines `Coslice` and the file's header essay says in prose (line 82) that
"pointed sets are the coslice of Set under the one-point set".

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.9) Instantiate `Construction/Slice.v:169`'s `Coslice` at
      `Sets` and the terminal object to obtain `Sets_*`, and prove it agrees
      with the direct (carrier + base point + point-preserving map)
      presentation — turning the header prose into a theorem.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.10 Exercise 6, printed page 187 (PDF
page 196), item `awodey:7:ex6` — show that a natural transformation is an
isomorphism in the functor category exactly when each component is, and decide
whether the analogous statement holds for monomorphisms. The monomorphism half
is the same obligation as pointwise monos and epis in a functor category.

The isomorphism half is in-tree, in existential form: `Instance/Fun.v:255`
`Theorem Functor_Setoid_Nat_Iso `(F G : C ⟶ D) : F ≅[Fun] G ↔ F ≈ G`, where
`F ≈ G` unfolds (`Theory/Functor.v:148`) to a componentwise-iso family
satisfying naturality. `rg 'Monic|Epic'` over `Instance/Fun.v`,
`Instance/Fun/Cartesian.v` and `Theory/Natural/Transformation.v` returns 0 hits.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.10 Ex 6) The isomorphism half stated as a predicate on a
      GIVEN transformation θ ("θ is invertible in `[C, D]` iff every θ_x is
      invertible in `D`"), rather than only the existential
      `F ≅[Fun] G ↔ F ≈ G`, so that invertibility of a particular θ can be read
      off directly instead of routed through `equiv_iso`.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.10 Exercise 11, printed page 188 (PDF
page 197), item `awodey:7:ex11` — determine which sorts of properties of
categories fail to respect equivalence, and exhibit one that is invariant under
isomorphism of categories but not under equivalence. Same obligation family as
skeletons and skeletal categories, where the canonical such property lives.

In-tree the observation exists only as prose: `Theory/Equivalence.v:92-97`
remarks that "skeletality is not equivalence-invariant", and the other
invariance comments (`Construction/Funny.v:40` and the `Funny/` satellites,
`Instance/StrictCat/Funny.v:38`, `Theory/Isomorphism.v:69`,
`Structure/Discrete.v:20`, `Theory/Displayed.v:90`) likewise state without
proving. No separating pair of equivalent categories is exhibited anywhere.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.10 Ex 11) A proved separation: a concrete pair of
      equivalent categories, one satisfying a property (e.g. skeletality, or
      "has exactly one object") and the other not — turning
      `Theory/Equivalence.v:92-97`'s prose into a theorem.

### Also covered by

Awodey, *Category Theory* (2nd ed.), §7.10 Exercise 12, printed page 188 (PDF
page 197), item `awodey:7:ex12` — call a category skeletal when isomorphic
objects are identical, and show that every category is equivalent to a skeletal
subcategory of itself. Same obligation as the skeletons/skeletal-categories
issue filed here.

In-tree there is prose and instances but no theorem: `Theory/Equivalence.v:92-99`
states the result and its equivalence with the axiom of choice, and says the
library "confines skeletons to concrete instances such as `Instance/FinSet.v`";
`Test/Poset.v:102` and `:150` prove two specific posets skeletal;
`Instance/FinSet.v:15-20` declares `FinSet` skeletal.

What this section adds:

- [ ] (from Awodey §7.10 Ex 12) State the skeleton theorem in the library's
      axiom-free-conditional style, over an explicit choice hypothesis rather
      than a global `Axiom`, since "every category has a skeleton" is
      equivalent to AC — the caveat already recorded at
